title: Kissar (bowl lyre)
summary: The kissar is the bowl lyre of the Nile valley. A round wooden bowl is covered with hide and laced at the edge; two slim arms rise from it and carry a crossbar, and five strings run from leather-wrapped ties on the bar down over a bridge to a tail cord. It is plucked with the fingers to accompany songs.
howToPlay: Five strings run from the crossbar down to the bridge, the lowest on the left. Each lane marks a place to pluck a string.
A bead slides down a string. Pluck the lane just as the bead lands on it.
The tunes are built from the five notes of the scale in short phrases that answer one another.
Learn a phrase first by echo, then play it along with the pulse.
rules: The five strings are tuned to a five-note scale with no half steps.
A stroke on the beat is perfect, a near one is good, and extra strokes cost points.
The phrases count four beats to the bar.
heritageNote: Bowl lyres have been made along the Nile for thousands of years. The kissar is still played in Nubian villages, where the bowl is often carved from a single piece of wood and covered with fresh hide each season.
credits: Tradition: the kissar lyre; phrases written for this game
